chapters.title: Chapter 2: How Startup Funding Rounds Work

lessons.title: The Funding Ladder: Pre-Seed, Seed, Series A and Beyond

children.text: In January 2021, a quick-commerce startup called Zepto raised its first round of about $730,000. By August 2023 it was valued at $1.4 billion, and a year later at $5 billion. That is the funding ladder climbed at record speed. Most startups climb it far more slowly, and most never get past the first rung or two. This lesson explains what each rung of the ladder is meant to prove, how big rounds typically are, how much ownership each one costs, how many companies fall off along the way, and what happens when a company has to step down a rung instead of up.

body.text: Every funding round is a trade: the company sells a slice of ownership to buy enough time and money to prove the next thing. Round names like seed and Series A are just labels for how much has been proven so far.

children.text: What Each Rung Must Prove

markDefs.definition: How many months a startup can keep operating with the cash it has, before it must raise money, become profitable or shut down.
The percentage of the company sold to new investors in a round, which reduces every existing shareholder's ownership by the same proportion.

children.text: Founders usually raise enough to cover 18 to 24 months of
runway
. In that time, they must hit the milestones the next set of investors will demand. Each round sells new shares, which causes
dilution
for everyone already on the cap table, including you.

body.title: Why round names are not reliable

children.text: "Seed" and "Series A" are not legal terms. No regulator defines them. One company's seed round can be larger than another's Series A, and you will see labels like pre-Series A, Series A1 or seed extension. Some founders call a round Series A to sound more mature. Ignore the label and ask what the company has actually achieved: revenue, growth rate, customer retention and how long the cash will last.
Following KhetSetu Up the Ladder

In Chapter 1, you put ₹10 lakh into KhetSetu's angel round at a ₹10 crore post-money valuation and got 1%. Now assume everything goes right and it climbs three more rungs. Every round dilutes you by the share of the company sold in that round:

body.caption: At seed, KhetSetu raises ₹8 crore at a ₹40 crore post-money valuation: 1% × (1 − 8 ÷ 40) = 1% × 0.8 = 0.8%.

body.title: Paper value of your ₹10 lakh after each round (₹ lakh, illustrative)

body.text: Your stake roughly halved from 1% to 0.52%, yet its paper value rose more than 40 times. That is dilution working in your favour: each round was priced higher than the last. But "paper value" is exactly that. ₹4.16 crore is only real if someone actually buys your shares at that price, and Chapter 3 shows how rarely and slowly that happens.

body.title: A bigger seed round
body.prompt: Suppose KhetSetu's seed round instead raised ₹10 crore at the same ₹40 crore post-money valuation. Starting from your 1%, what would your stake be after this round?
body.explanation: Dilution = ₹10 crore ÷ ₹40 crore = 25%. New stake = 1% × (1 − 0.25) = 0.75%. Raising more money at the same valuation gives the company more runway, but costs every existing shareholder a bigger slice.

children.text: How Many Companies Fall Off the Ladder

The KhetSetu table is the dream path. Reality is harsher. Global venture data from sources such as Carta suggests that historically only around 20 to 30% of seed-funded companies went on to raise a Series A, and recent cohorts have done worse. Some estimates put the typical gap between a seed round and a Series A in India at around 20 months, which means a seed-stage company must survive close to two years on its last cheque while hitting its targets.

body.title: What the ladder means for you
body.question: If you back 10 seed-stage startups and the illustrative numbers above hold, what should you expect?
options: Most of them will reach Series A, because they already raised a seed round
About 2 will raise a Series A, and the other 8 are at high risk of returning little or nothing
All 10 will exit eventually, just at different valuations
body.explanation: At a 20% graduation rate, roughly 2 of 10 will raise a Series A. The rest may survive as small businesses, get sold cheaply or shut down, and in most of those cases angels recover little. The numbers are illustrative, not a forecast for any specific portfolio.

children.text: When the Ladder Breaks: Bridge Rounds and Down Rounds

markDefs.definition: A smaller, stopgap round, often from existing investors, to extend runway until the company can raise its next full round.
A round priced at a lower valuation than the company's previous round.

children.text: Not every company moves smoothly upward. When a startup runs short of cash before hitting its milestones, it often raises a
bridge round
from existing investors to buy a few more months. If growth has disappointed, the next round may be a
down round

. Say KhetSetu's seed round was at a ₹40 crore post-money valuation, but it misses its revenue targets and can only raise its Series A at a ₹30 crore pre-money valuation. New investors now pay less per share than the seed investors did, and existing shareholders absorb the hit.

columns.label: Up round
points: New price per share is higher than the last round
Dilution is offset by a rise in the value of your shares
Signals the company hit its milestones
Makes the next round easier to raise

columns.label: Down round
points: New price per share is lower than the last round
You are diluted and your shares are worth less
Signals missed targets or a tougher funding market
Can trigger protection clauses for later investors that hurt early angels most

body.text: Down rounds usually hit angels hardest. Later investors often negotiate anti-dilution protection, which gives them extra shares if a future round is priced lower, and those extra shares come out of everyone else's ownership. Angels on plain equity shares rarely have that protection. Chapter 4 covers these clauses in detail.

children.text: Zepto: The Ladder at Record Speed

stats.label: Valuation a year later
stats.context: August 2024, $340 million round led by General Catalyst

children.text: Zepto, founded by Aadit Palicha and Kaivalya Vohra, went from its first cheque to a $5 billion valuation in about three and a half years, raising multiple large rounds in quick succession. Remember it as the exception that makes headlines, not the benchmark. Many solid Indian startups take seven to ten years to reach late-stage funding, and a far larger number never reach Series A at all.

body.label: Where most angels enter
body.context: This is where valuations are lowest and potential multiples are highest, and also where the most companies fall off the ladder.

body.title: Ananya's two offers
body.scenario:
Ananya, an HNI in Ahmedabad, is offered two deals in the same week.
Deal A: a pre-seed healthtech startup with a working app and 2,000 free users, raising at a ₹15 crore post-money valuation.
Deal B: a seed-stage B2B software company with ₹6 crore in annual revenue that tripled in the last year, raising at a ₹60 crore post-money valuation.
Her friend says Deal A is obviously better because the valuation is four times lower.
body.prompt: Is her friend right? What should Ananya think about before choosing?
body.modelAnswer:
1. A lower valuation is not automatically cheaper. Deal A is priced lower because far less has been proven: it has free users, no revenue and must climb more rungs of the ladder before any exit.
2. Deal B costs more per unit of ownership but has already proven customers will pay and that revenue is growing fast.
3. Ignoring future dilution, a 10x return needs Deal A to be worth ₹150 crore and Deal B to be worth ₹600 crore. Deal A needs a smaller outcome but has a much higher chance of never getting there.
4. For each deal she should ask: how many months of runway will this round buy, what exactly must be proven before the next round, and does the valuation match the traction?
5. Neither deal is better by its label or its price. The right choice depends on which risk she understands and can judge better, and both should be small cheques within a diversified plan.

body.title: Name the round
body.textWithBlank: A funding round priced at a lower valuation than the company's previous round is called a ___ round.
body.explanation: A down round means new investors pay less per share than earlier investors did. It usually signals missed milestones or a harder funding market, and it tends to hurt early, unprotected shareholders the most.

cards.definition: The earliest outside round, usually funding a prototype to prove people want the product.
A round that funds early revenue and proves the company can find customers repeatedly.
The first large institutional VC round, funding a business model that has shown consistent growth.
How many months a startup can operate on its current cash before it must raise money or become profitable.
A smaller stopgap round, often from existing investors, that extends runway until the next full round.
A round priced at a lower valuation than the company's previous round.

points: Each funding round sells ownership to buy 18 to 24 months of runway to prove the next milestone.
Round names are loose labels; judge a company by revenue, growth and runway, not by what it calls its round.
Each round dilutes existing shareholders: new stake = old stake × (1 − new money ÷ post-money valuation).
Up rounds can multiply the paper value of a shrinking stake, but paper value is not cash until someone buys your shares.
Only a minority of seed-funded companies reach Series A, so most angel cheques face their biggest risk in the first two years.
Bridge and down rounds are warning signs, and down rounds usually hurt early angels more than protected later investors.
